idiom_name: test-only function with the collaborator's signature, wired in through a function pointer
implementation_notes: C has no objects and no mocking runtime, so the Test Stub degenerates into Meszaros' Procedural Test Stub: the collaborator is reached through a function pointer (or a small struct of function pointers) that production code takes as an argument, and the test supplies a test-only function that returns the canned value, so the real symbol is never called. Where the collaborator is a plain extern function rather than an injected pointer, the substitution happens at link time - the test executable is linked against a stub definition with the same signature (weak symbol or a test-only translation unit) instead of the production object file. Keep the answers in the stub function itself (or in a file-scope variable the test sets before exercising the SUT) and reset that state between tests.
pitfalls: A direct extern call compiled into the production object is not redirected by a stub merely present in the test; the call must go through the pointer (or be resolved weakly at link time), otherwise the real function runs.
State kept in file-scope variables survives from one test function to the next; reset the stub's globals in setup (fff's RESET_FAKE/FFF_RESET_HISTORY exist for exactly this).
Function-pointer parameters spelled inline (e.g. a callback type inside the fake declaration) expand into illegal declarations; give the test a typedef for any function-pointer parameter.

variants.name: Generated fake functions via the Fake Function Framework (or CMock)
variants.implementation_notes: fff is a single header: FAKE_VALUE_FUNC(int, has_inventory, const char *, int) declares the fake function and a companion struct whose return_val field holds the canned answer, and RESET_FAKE restores it between tests; CMock generates equivalent fakes ahead of time from the production header, with optional expectation plugins. Both replace the hand-written function plus its glue, and both keep the call history a test may inspect afterwards. Choose the generated form when a module exposes many functions or the test also wants call counts; the value-returning field - not expectation verification - is what keeps it a stub rather than a mock.
pitfalls: FFF macros declare and define the fake in one step, so placing one in a shared header produces duplicate definitions; declare in a header and define in one test source instead.
Fakes are global by default: reset them per test (RESET_FAKE) or the previous test's return_val answers the next test's calls.
A fake with a function-pointer parameter needs a typedef visible to the test, because the macro expands the parameter into a variable declaration.
